il_d_beaver_wall.blurb: Beaver Wall is a steep sport wall in the North Canyon at Jackson Falls, in the Shawnee National Forest of southern Illinois, a short walk from the falls and not far north of the Mr. Jimmy boulder. The overhanging sandstone face holds 14 climbs, nearly all bolted, with a single trad line. Difficulty runs high: a cluster of 5.12s and a few 5.13s make up most of the wall, with a pair of 5.11s, and only three easier lines at 5.8 and 5.9 for warming up. Sun reaches it from morning through afternoon, so choose a cooler day, since Jackson Falls summers run hot and humid.

il_f_dynasty_wall.blurb: Dynasty Wall is a sport wall at Jackson Falls in the Shawnee National Forest, southern Illinois, filed under the West Falls section of the canyon. It has 15 bolted routes and leans toward the hard end: two 5.9s and a lone 5.10, then a strong run of 5.11 to 5.13 climbs, topped by one 5.14. Climbers looking for it should head just past the Battle Ax wall, short of The Munchkin boulder. Jackson Falls is a forested sandstone canyon, so expect shade, though summers are humid.

il_j_saccharine_cliffline.blurb: Saccharine Cliffline is a compact bouldering stretch within the Holy Boulders, in Jackson County in southern Illinois, where the sandstone is known for good friction. It sits on the east side of the path between the Public Enemy and Illuminati zones, with a big roof low on the cliffline. Of its 15 climbs, 14 are boulder problems and one is a top-rope line. Problems run mostly from V5 to V6 with a few easier ones and a couple of hard tests up to V9, and the style leans on roofs, traverses and cracks, so finger locks and lie-backs get plenty of use.

il_i_bee_wall.blurb: Bee Wall is a tall, exposed stretch of the main cliff in Mississippi Palisades State Park, on the Illinois bank of the Mississippi River, between Indian Head and the Amphitheater. It carries 15 climbs, almost all trad with a single top-rope line, and the grades are friendly: mostly 5.5 to 5.9 with just one 5.10. The routes are less traveled, so some hold dirt and loose rock and are worth testing as you go. Natural anchors above are common here, and the park as a whole is best in the cooler, drier autumn months.
